item.title: Staying sane while trying to save the world: Highlights from Spencer Greenberg and Luisa Rodriguez
item.description:
Many people have found value in this 80,000 Hours podcast episode from July 2026: Spencer Greenberg on staying sane while trying to save the world. 

The highlights below are Julia's picks of the best bits, lightly reformatted, for those who prefer a written format. Thanks to Spencer, Luisa, and 80,000 Hours for allowing me to republish their material! Most quotes are from Spencer, and some are from Luisa.

Nutshell version at 80,000 Hours: 5 minute read
Medium version below: 17 minute read
Full podcast at 80,000 Hours: 2 hour listen, or read the full transcript

………….

Spencer Greenberg — founder of ClearerThinking.org and coauthor of The 12 Levers: The Complete Psychological Toolkit for Improving Your Life — talks with Luisa Rodriguez about the psychological toll of working on existential risk, AI safety, factory farming, and other high-stakes problems.

Drawing on a recent survey his team ran, he argues that grinding yourself down is self-defeating even on its own terms, and that the way out runs through understanding your actual psychology rather than forcing an idealised one. He and Luisa discuss practical, evidence-based tools from his new book, The 12 Levers, that can help with the most common challenges.

………….

What people report helps them

At the top of the list are: therapy, medication, talking to friends and family about the issues. 

We surveyed people who work on these high-impact cause areas like existential risk, animal welfare, and AI. We ended up getting about 60 to 110 respondents, depending on the question. A lot of the most instructive stuff was around when we asked the question, “What would you advise someone who’s very similar to you who’s getting into this field, in terms of dealing with these psychological challenges?”

  1. Many people talked about sustainability, and how focusing on sustainability is really important. Even if you don’t think it matters for its own sake, it’s really important just to be effective. And people that are very focused on sacrifice rather than sustainability often aren’t even able to achieve the thing they want. In other words, sacrifice doesn’t work over the long term, leads to boom-and-bust cycles, or they burn out and they end up having to leave or change their work.

    Being totally adherent to a philosophy can actually increase people’s self-deception around this. If you think that everything has to be justified in terms of maximising utility, then now, given your nature as a human being, you have tremendous psychological pressure to justify everything that is for something else you care about in terms of maximising utility. And I think that’s actually a very unhealthy and self-deluded state to be in.

    But if you accept, “Wait, I’m a human. I have multiple values, and here’s what I actually value,” then you can talk about,“Actually, the reason I have my friends is because I value human connection, it’s really important to me, and they bring me joy, not because it makes me more effective.” 
     
  2. People really encourage others to have life outside of the work. In other words, to build relationships that are not just all people in the community.

    Maintaining relationships outside of people in the community, that can give you a break, that can give you a playful experience that’s not just about work. Because maybe when you’re socialising with people who also prioritise these topics, there’s a natural tendency for them to come up all the time, even when you’re supposed to be doing restful things.
     
  3. Don’t wait until things have fallen apart. Be preventative about taking care of yourself. Notice the earliest signs of pre-burnout. Don’t wait until it’s burnout.

    Like, “I’m noticing I have a bit less motivation here. I’m noticing that I’m waking up stressed every day, or I’m having trouble sleeping.” And then take preventative action — whether that’s seeing a therapist, seeing a coach, just doing self-improvement techniques to try to improve that situation — and not saying, “Well, I can live with this bad sleep, I can live with this feeling of stress all the time, I can live with this lower motivation.” Maybe, but is it going to get worse, and how long can you actually live with it? And also, you don’t necessarily have to live with it. You can have a more pleasant lifestyle. You don’t have to necessarily suffer so much, and you still might be able to be equally or more effective.

Accepting limitations

Even if your goal were just to get the maximum performance, you have to be realistic about what kind of body you have and what kind of mind you have — and grinding all the way is not actually the way to get maximum performance. It’s a naive version of trying to get maximum performance. 

We’re such limited beings, and that no matter how hard we work to be unlimited beings, we’re never going to get there. All of these things are just ideals that we strive for and we won’t come close.

For example, I really care about trying to be rational, and I regularly see how far I am from that goal. And you could let that kind of undercut your motivation, being like, “Oh man, I’m so far from that,” or you can turn that around and you can say, “Hey, I can keep becoming a better version of myself and move incrementally towards this more ideal form.” And that can be exciting. I don’t think it has to be demotivating. It can be motivating, actually: being limited, but seeing how you can progress and improve.

But I would also say that failing to accept your limitations can actually be disastrous towards the goals that you care about. So the more accurately you can see yourself — what you are, what your limitations are — the better you can be at all the things that you care about. 

Responding to alarming evidence

What is hypervigilance, and what’s the point of it? Effectively, it’s a state that’s preparing you to take drastic action. Like there’s something dangerous that’s coming: you’ve got to go, you’ve got to act. Unfortunately, it’s really not a healthy state to be in all the time. It’s not good for your body, it’s not good for your mind. It actually affects your digestion when you’re in a hypervigilant state.

I like to think about professional athletes here. Do professional athletes want to be stressing their bodies all the time? If you’re training to be in the Olympics, and all you care about is the goal of winning the Olympics, are you just stressing your body to the absolute limit? The answer is absolutely no, because that is not the performance-optimising move. The performance-optimising move involves genuine rest; it involves variation of things. You’re not always working just on that one skill set. You’re going to have off days. You’re going to have days where you’re practicing other things or doing cross training or whatever — and that’s even if you just care about optimising for the goal.”

News 

When people feel like there’s a frightening thing in the world, they’ll often track it. You look at early days of the COVID pandemic, people were absolutely glued to any source of information, couldn’t talk about anything else. And I think it is that vigilant system of like, “This really scary thing is there. We’ve all got to monitor it really closely.”

You need a system for monitoring it. That is important if that’s your field, if that’s what you’re focused on. But once you have that in place, it actually can give you permission to not monitor other times

Let’s say you’re in the field of AI, and things are moving so fast. It may be even more difficult to deal with, just because there is information you really want to stay on top of and it is changing a lot. And there, I would say the same kind of strategy can be useful: being really aware of where am I getting my news, what are the good news sources, what’s the stuff that’s going to keep me up to date?

And then trying to block out all the noise. You don’t need to constantly scroll down and get every single new post on X about AI, a bunch of which are probably complete exaggerations anyway or bad takes. You know, figure out your trusted news sources and that’s where you’re going to get your information. 

False rest and real rest

People go to social media as a form of avoidance or as a form of attempting to unwind, right? So they’re like, “I don’t want to think about this thing. I’m stuck on this thing. Let me open up social media.” Or like, “I’ve just been working hard, let me unwind.” And the irony is that they end up often in this sort of hypervigilant state when they’re on social media, where it’s like not even necessarily doing a good job of getting them to relax, or maybe they’ve avoided this one thing and now they’re stressed out about this other thing they’re looking at.

What else is restful? What else shares that same need? Maybe walking your dog or going for a walk in nature or having a call with a friend or whatever it is. And maybe it takes a little bit more planning to make that happen; it’s not quite as mindless — but if you could swap it out with something that serves the same need at least as well, hopefully better, but where afterwards you’re like, “I’m glad I did that; that was a good use of time,” it can not only serve our needs better, but actually make life more meaningful and fulfilling, and I think be more restorative.

You need to do meaningful work, that’s great, but you’re trying to replace your need to rest, and it doesn’t satisfy your need to rest. It’s a different thing. And actually, you can kind of grind yourself to a pulp and make it hard for you to function if you’re never letting yourself actually satisfy that rest need. Or if your “rest” is not actually restful, like you’re actually stressed out doing your rest because you’re scrolling stressful AI news or whatever it is.

Motivation: clean fuel and dirty fuel

Based on Spencer’s interview with Stephen Zerfas on the Clearer Thinking podcast, about motivation.

How are we motivating ourselves to get stuff done?

A lot of really high-achieving people use what [Zerfas] calls “dirty fuel,” which is essentially we beat ourselves up or are really harsh on ourselves as a way to get really good performance. And the irony of it is often it does work for people, but it has tremendous psychological costs, and also it can be unsustainable. It might actually be bad in the long run where they burn out or actually don’t achieve their goals because of the psychological costs. And then there’s this idea of “clean fuel,” which is other ways to motivate yourself that don’t have the psychological costs, or even have psychological benefits.

Being human, there are a lot of ways we can motivate ourselves. One of them is telling ourselves we’re never doing enough or feeling guilt, but we can have other forms of motivation. We could have social motivation: maybe I’ll collaborate with someone, and that will motivate me. We can have reward-based motivation: if I do this, I’ll give myself this cool reward. Et cetera, et cetera. There are many forms of motivation. I could try to develop a feeling of excitement around this project in particular. I don’t think there’s like a switch we can flip, but we can experiment in small ways on lower-stakes things on other ways to motivate ourselves

Boom and bust cycles

There can be a kind of boom-and-bust cycle of periods of giving work kind of everything you’ve got, sprinting really hard, but then neglecting your own needs and eventually crashing.

How would you want to act in these difficult situations? What would the ideal version of you do? Let’s say you think that there’s a really high chance that existential risk is on the horizon. Suppose you believe that. Would you want yourself to just be freaked out 100% of the time? Is that actually the ideal version of you? And what is the ideal version of you? How often would you be freaked out, and to what degree? And what would that fear do for you?

When you kind of do that thought experiment, you realise that actually just being freaked out all the time is like, on some level it feels maybe proportionate to you, but it’s actually not what you would want of yourself. And the ideal version of you wouldn’t be in that state.

Imagine you had a magic dial and you could control how much of different emotions you would feel. Let’s take your fear: where would you dial that dial?

[People] sometimes feel like therapists are trying to push them down to zero. Not that that’s achievable, but they might feel that, and they may actually have resistance to that because they might feel like zero is not the right level.

So I’d ask that of you: would you actually leave the dial exactly where it is?

[About guilt]: what is it detecting in the smoke detector model? It’s detecting a feeling like you’ve done wrong or you’ve violated a moral standard. And then I would ask the question: have you really? Like, I don’t know how much you work, but is working 80 hours required as a moral standard? Should everyone feel guilty for not working 80 hours if they could make a difference, like you believe you can, et cetera?

What is this guilt doing for you, and what’s its cost? On that magic dial, how much guilt would you choose to feel? Would you choose to feel the amount on the magic dial if you could control it? Is the guilt actually helping you do a better job, or is it actually impairing you and making you do a worse job?

Specialness

My own kind of cycles of sprinting really hard, feeling like I have this sense of duty to do as much as I can, is related to feeling like I’m special; that I might be one of a few people who can make a difference to whether we solve these global problems.

So a bit of a savior complex. It feels kind of uncomfortably entangled with feelings of grandiosity and narcissism, which feels yucky saying aloud. But yeah, I find myself attached to the idea that me specifically, I might have a lot to contribute. It feels kind of related to having to main character energy.

And the fact that I’m really beating myself up for not eking out a few extra hours a week to work does just feel like it’s really coming from this “maybe I’m special and I’m going to make a difference.” Whereas really, realistically, I think the more correct thing is, “I am playing my part. My part is not enormous. Whether I work a few extra hours this week is not going to save the world or determine whether things go well or badly.”

Agency

The survey actually had kind of a striking pattern, where people said their anxiety went down once they started actually working on the problem — that doing something, even something small, was more bearable than just passively dreading. For some people, there’s something like agency that is actually really helpful for them.

Getting really pragmatic and just working on the behavior can often make people feel a lot better. And that tracks with “find a problem and go work on it,” even if you have this existential angst.

We’re talking about different probabilities of different outcomes — and I would be very surprised if there’s absolutely no chance that we succeed at our goals. I think there’s some chance at least that things could go well.

And I find it helpful to think about how I’m going to help in the set of worlds where this is a tractable problem. I’m not going to help in the set of worlds where it isn’t tractable and we’re doomed from the start. I’m also not going to help in the set of worlds where it isn’t a problem at all. But in the set of worlds where what we can do could make a difference, I’m going to play a part, and that’s really meaningful.

So I let go, and I feel sad about the worlds where I couldn’t have done anything at all to make a difference, but I act as if I’m in the worlds where I can — because that’s all I can do, really.

Coping with fear of death / extinction

Do the coping strategies that help with individual death help with the extinction of humanity?

We really have to grapple with the enormity of the value loss that would actually be tremendously bad. And I think the way to cope with it is not to pretend it’s less bad than it is. But an interesting thing is that even things that are really, really bad, you can become more psychologically strong in the face of them.

Think about people going into battle for some just cause. Let’s say their people are being attacked and they have to defend their people. And you think of, for example, a courageous warrior going into battle: they might die, their whole family might be wiped out, their entire community and their whole civilisation might be wiped out — but it doesn’t mean that they have to go in in terror. And in fact, going into that battle in terror is dysfunctional: it actually makes it more likely that they’re going to get wiped out, right?

So I think we need to understand that the enormity of something being difficult does not imply you have to just be in terror all the time.

Different psychological strategies that are helpful for different people. One of them is going to be around courage, and this idea of being strong in the face of adversity and standing up to difficult things. For some people, that can actually be inspiring in a way.

For others, the best strategy will be acceptance. But acceptance does not mean that you’re not resisting it and trying to stop it. Acceptance is a psychological attitude of, “I accept that this thing is a possibility. My mind is not rebelling against reality, but that doesn’t mean I’m not going to work my hardest to fight it. In fact, I might be more effective fighting it if I accept it.”

A useful metaphor here is: imagine a patient that is likely to be terminally ill. Like, they have a high probability of being terminally ill, but there’s still some stuff they can do to increase the probability of survival. Let’s say they have a year to live, but it’s a chance to survive if they can do everything right, but they probably won’t no matter what they do.

What is the best attitude for the patient to have? There will be some individual variation, but I think one healthy attitude would be to try to fully accept the possibility that they’re going to die — so they’re no longer mentally rebelling against that while still taking effective action to reduce that probability.

The word “acceptance” is a little funny there, because we don’t mean “accept” as in, “OK, I’m fine with it; I’m not going to resist it.” We mean “accept” in that you’re no longer mentally rebelling against it. You’re no longer saying, “This can’t be happening. I won’t accept this. Fuck this.” You’re saying, “Here’s reality. And now I’m going to operate under the assumption of reality.”

When other people don’t get it

We can actually still have really good relationships, even if we have these differences in important beliefs. 

There’s ways to talk about it where you talk about it more in terms of your experience, rather than in the conversation requiring they buy into a set of assumptions.

With animals, it might be that you saw something that disturbed you. And you can say, “I saw this thing and I felt really disturbed by it.” That’s not making a factual claim about the objective nature of this problem, but it’s like, I was really bothered by this, and then they can relate to the fact that you are bothered and connect over that.

Or let’s say with AI, maybe your friends and family have other concerns about AI, and they’re not the same as yours. You could talk about it in a broader way. Say, “I’m really concerned about AI. In my job, I have to think about it all the time, and actually I find it disturbing to think about.” You don’t have to get into the exact facts and then negotiate what’s actually true. A lot of our friends and family, they want to connect with us and they want us to feel better and they want to empathise with us. But we can accidentally derail it by making it about the facts.

There’s incredible amounts of disagreement around these topics, so if you’re super duper confident you’ve got the correct answer, it’s worth being a little bit epistemically humble. 

Very rarely are people willing to be convinced unless they could see the possibility that they could convince you too, right? If I come in, like, “Here’s why you’re wrong,” you’re not going to listen to me. But if I’m like, “Let me hear you out. I want to hear your perspective. Can I also tell you my perspective?” Now we can actually have a real dialogue.

Balancing impact and personal wellbeing

Whether to have kids, work/life balance, personal spending versus donating, saving for retirement, doing a job you find difficult or unenjoyable, where to live, risk tolerance in career choices. It's kind of just one question over and over again: how much of your life are you allowed to keep for yourself versus do you want to spend on solving global problems?

​​You probably really care about sentient beings not suffering and the world not ending. Those are probably deep, important things that connect to your intrinsic values. And you also care about connection to your loved ones and maintaining your relationship with them, and having pleasure in your life, and not suffering yourself too much.

So then we can now ask the empirical question: how much do you care about each of those? And the answer to that is not going to be a stable number. In my experience, just as a claim about human psychology, that is going to depend on to what extent you’re neglecting each of them. If you are investing all your focus on reducing suffering in the world, there’s a good chance that the other values will pull a lot harder. And if you really inspect, you’re going to say, “These are mattering more now to me because I neglected them. I’ve not been satisfying these values.”

Then the way I approach it is I try to strike a balance between these things. I try to not neglect my intrinsic values, but let them sort of come in communication with each other and find a balance between them that feels right. And that’s a psychological quest. It’s not a quest about the nature of philosophy or the universe.

When someone is all-in on the mission, and only thinks about the mission and doesn’t take into account their other values: they start to pull harder on them psychologically, and I think that leads to things like burnout. I think one of the causes of burnout is neglecting your other important values.  

I think you’ll pay a very significant price to not understand your values.

[More in the episode about Spencer’s approach: valuism]

Parts work

[On various approaches to understanding what different parts of you want]

The classic general technique is you want to notice that there’s some part of you that wants something or has urges or needs not met. You can give it a name. It can be helpful to give it a name, because then you can talk about it or refer to it later. So maybe you’ll say, like, “I’m going to call it the Critic. It’s the part of me that tells me I’m never doing enough, I’m never good enough.”

And then you want to put yourself into a state where you can talk to it very compassionately, without being reactive. And they give different names to this, like the Self or the Compassionate Self or the Adult or whatever it is. But you’re kind of going to be dialoguing with this part from a very compassionate, healthy state, and you’re going to try to just explore what that part needs and wants and cares about, and try to help it have its needs met.

I had to kind of grieve the part of me that wanted to work 80-hour weeks because it thought that was the most morally good thing to do in order to fulfil the wishes of the part of me that really wanted to be a mom. And I think that part of me that wanted to work harder would have just kept being like, “You’re a bad person! You’re a bad person!” unless I’d really heard it out and been like, “I hear you. Thank you. You want me to be a good person, I appreciate that. But I’ve decided, full-eyed looking honestly at things, that I want to be a mom anyways.”

..............

Full episode at 80,000 Hours. 

Spencer's new book, The 12 Levers, teaches related psychological tools in concrete terms.



Discuss

item.title: A Chinese Perspective on “On Social Reality in China”
item.description:
I think “On Social Reality in China” makes many accurate observations, but I find the comparison fundamentally uneven. There are already many interesting comments there, but they’re too scattered, so I’m starting a separate post to respond in a more systematic and comprehensive way.

The most critical blind spot is this: the author draws on his familiarity with Western liberal middle-class intellectual circles, yet primarily understands China through pop culture and the experiences of the previous generation of immigrants. This is hardly fair. China has always had many small, highly self-selected communities of intellectuals, much like LessWrong itself. Since we’re looking for rationalists—regardless of which country they come from—why judge them by their country’s pop culture?

I’ll respond to the author’s four axes one by one, then discuss why rationalist and EA communities are harder to build in China. Briefly, I believe that censorship mechanisms and speech controls affect independent organizations far more than China’s broader cultural context does. Under these circumstances, even when people with similar interests and beliefs come together, it’s difficult for them to build anything—I’ve seen far too many examples.

About me: born in China in the mid-1990s, grew up in a middle-class family in one of the major cities, and might be on the autism spectrum. I moved to Western Europe before the pandemic and now live in France. My perspective is limited too, but I know many Chinese intellectual communities that care about knowledge, truth, social justice, and technology ethics.

Contents

1. Chinese social media is like social media everywhere.

2. “The primacy of social reality” is not relevant here.

3. “The Dark World frame” is not a fixed cultural phenomenon, but a product of its time, and it’s changing.

4. “Chinese nationalism as collective insecurity” is the section I agree with the most—let’s take a deeper look.

5. In China, people with backgrounds in the humanities and social sciences are more enthusiastic about engaging in public discourse than those with backgrounds in STEM. Continue to produce high-quality translations—even if they don’t help with policymaking, they allow people to see one another.

Chinese Social Media Is Like Social Media Everywhere

The author looks at mainstream Chinese social media through its lowest-quality content, while his view of the West comes from a very different intellectual environment. 

Beauty filters, anxiety about body image, a flood of low-quality books and films, and internet users’ pursuit of exposure and attention—aren’t these things also obviously present on YouTube, Instagram, Reddit, and TikTok? These issues have long been serious topics of research in the US and Europe, and the same is true in China.

Jonathan Haidt discussed many of these problems in his Atlantic article “Why the Past 10 Years of American Life Have Been Uniquely Stupid.” He describes how likes, shares, and recommendation algorithms reward emotional content and encourage people to perform for audiences. Chinese media have been criticizing these problems too. Sanlian Life Weekly has published in-depth reports on the logic of capital behind the mini-drama industry and the phenomena it has created: “How Do Viral Mini-Dramas Spark a Traffic Frenzy?” and the podcast episode “The Mini-Drama Assembly Line.” In China’s intellectual circles, such reflections are by no means uncommon.

Critiquing low-quality popular entertainment is a timeless topic among intellectuals worldwide. In today’s world, if you can use high-quality content to deconstruct such extremely widespread and absurd material, you can also attract a large audience and profit from it. China has no shortage of such content creators and influencers.

There is no evidence to suggest that the widespread problems caused by social media are more severe in China than elsewhere. But more importantly, what do any of these observations tell us about the people rationalist communities hope to reach? LessWrong didn't turn itself into Twitter to attract more readers, did it?

I suspect the author would never actively seek out the most superficial content on Western social media, just as I would never seek out the Chinese content he describes. Chinese is my first language, so I know how to find media, podcasts, and intellectual communities that align with my interests, and such resources are not scarce. However, seeking out, discerning, and consistently following these sources of information requires a considerable level of language proficiency and cultural familiarity. For overseas Chinese who primarily engage with China through family experiences and pop culture, this is neither easy nor, it seems, necessary.

Of course, Chinese and Western social media are not identical, especially given China’s strict censorship. But I would never go into a Chinese intellectual community and claim that Fox News and Instagram influencers represent American society. I'll spare you the screenshots.

The Primacy of Social Reality: How Is This Relevant?

Many of the things the author describes are real, but I don’t see how they are particularly relevant to finding rationalists in China. Still, I’d like to correct a few of his interpretations. I’ll leave some detailed points in the comments, since they would take us too far from the main theme.

I haven’t read The 48 Laws of Power, so I won’t comment on the book itself. But in fact, there has never been a shortage of reflection on the ideas this book seeks to convey. For centuries, literature from around the world—in English, French, Chinese, and other languages—has never lacked critical works addressing social structures, power dynamics, and manipulation. Think of Jane Austen, Edith Wharton, Guy de Maupassant, or Lu Xun. 

I do think that in East Asian societies such as China, Japan, and South Korea, the pressure stemming from “social norms” is stronger than in Western societies. However, there are significant differences across regions, just as there are within the West—for example, Britain is also known for its own strong traditions of social restraint. Still, none of this is relevant here.

I don’t know whether China’s current political system is historically inevitable (who knows?), but we cannot simply confuse “people’s circumstances” with “people’s beliefs.” Understanding these rules, using them (whether actively or passively), believing in them, and having the ability to change them—these are entirely different matters. If my mom said “Americans just love Trump,” I would definitely correct her.

The same goes for unspoken rules. Drinking culture, workplace hierarchies, bribery, and nepotism are all common in China. But when I watched House of Cards and Succession, those power games felt all too familiar. Still, I don’t see why any of this should matter when looking for rationalists. When I talk to people in rationalist communities, I’m interested in their ideas, not their position in some social hierarchy. I would never try to understand American rationalists by studying the social hierarchy of college fraternities or Wall Street.

In this regard, the differences between various industries and organizations are far more significant than geographical cultural differences. For example, drinking culture and relationship-based business practices can hardly be seen in Shenzhen’s tech industry, often called China’s Silicon Valley. I doubt most people in rationalist communities work in traditional industries, so why use traditional workplace culture to understand potential rationalists in China?

The Dark World Frame: A Product of Its Time

I do agree that the Dark World Frame the author describes is quite common in China, probably more so than in many Western countries. But I don’t think it’s a fixed feature of Chinese culture. This worldview has been strongly shaped by particular historical and economic conditions, and it is changing now.

I agree with w_jin’s comment about how economic reforms and mass migration disrupted traditional networks of trust in China. See Fei Xiaotong’s From the Soil From the Soil: The Foundations of Chinese Society, which describes how social relationships and trust worked in traditional rural China. His China’s Gentry: Essays on Rural-Urban Relations is also worth reading for its analysis of how China’s traditional social structures were changing long before these reforms:

Unfortunately China is still in the status of a semicolony. Large-scale industrial development is not feasible. The essence of Western civilization, industrialism, has not been really introduced as yet. What has been brought in is the superstructure of the more superficial elements of this civilization, including the desire for material comforts and satisfactions. But there has not been constructed as yet the material foundation on the basis of which these things would make sense. This lack of foundation creates a special class of people who live superficially in Western culture but without a traditional base from either the West or the East. These are both the victims and the directors of China’s tragedy.

— Fei Xiaotong, “Social Erosion in the Rural Communities,” in China’s Gentry: Essays on Rural-Urban Relations (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1953), pp. 139–140.

That was written between 1947 and 1948. Beyond Fei’s analysis, I’d like to add some more historical context. In 1949, the Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China—the China we know today. In the following years, the communist ideal provided many people with a framework for understanding fairness, personal sacrifice, and collectivism. Among the intellectuals who came of age in the 1930s and 1940s, many sincerely believed that a better world could be built through this new social system.

At that time, the Soviet Union had not yet collapsed, and resisting capitalism and realizing communism remained important goals for China. As for the phrase “saving lives and helping people”—for which the author’s wife was mocked by their Chinese friend—this spirit of universal love was precisely the kind of value that the government was promoting at the time.

But then came the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which caused enormous human suffering, and many people began to question the relationship between political ideals and reality. They paid a terrible price for different visions of a better world.

Then, in 1978, China began its economic reforms. Over the following decades, people saw themselves or those around them earning much more money, eating food they had never been able to afford, moving into better homes, buying cars, and traveling. My parents lived through all of this, and I grew up surrounded by people whose lives and values were shaped by these changes. I imagine the author's parents may have had similar experiences.

That generation tends to emphasize the role of individual effort in wealth accumulation, yet overlooks the fact that they are beneficiaries of the tide of history. Rapid social mobility created countless exciting opportunities, and the wealth gap widened rapidly. Compared to previous decades, economic success suddenly became the most attractive goal.

There is a form of intergenerational rebellion at play. The generation before them once believed in grand social ideals, only to experience social upheaval and the shattering of those ideals. As a result, the younger generation has reached a completely different conclusion: What good are ideals? Making money is what really matters. Rather than discussing how society should be, it’s better to focus on how to improve one’s own life.

This reminds me of the American Dream. When people believe they have a chance to become winners, they may accept the rules of competition even if those rules produce enormous inequality.

And in China, the cost of staying in that competition is enormous. I’m getting tired of explaining to my European friends that China’s education and work culture have long demanded far more time and effort than they’re used to. Students grow up with long hours of schoolwork, and adults face a widespread culture of working overtime. The right to rest, which European workers fought for over generations, is still poorly protected in China. For generations of Chinese people, this has been a normal part of life.

But this worldview changes as economic conditions change. In recent years, I’ve seen more discussion of workers’ rights, inequality, gender, and mental health in Chinese-language media. These concerns aren’t new; however, as the economy has slowed, such views have become easier to spread. The next round of intergenerational rebellion is just beginning.

Chinese Nationalism as Collective Insecurity: A Deeper Look

I agree that Chinese nationalism involves a strong sense of collective insecurity and a desire to prove China’s worth to the West. As a side note, I think China and Russia share many similarities in this regard. I’ve previously discussed the historical roots of Russian nationalism in a Chinese-language podcast, based on my research into the evolution of Russian architecture. Why not just discuss China directly? Because it would most likely be blocked by censorship. 

So, let me take this opportunity to talk a little about China. China suffered numerous foreign invasions in the 19th century. I don’t think I need to denounce the history of colonialism to a Western liberal intellectual community that values self-reflection so highly, do I?

In middle and high school history classes, we were taught about the immense cultural treasures of China’s millennia-long history, and then about how humiliating it was to be invaded by Western countries. This narrative is, of course, intended to reinforce a sense of national identity, as history education does in many countries. Building on this foundation, political classes emphasized the conflict between foreign capitalism and our socialism.

Hence we were constantly reminded of how China had been humiliated by Western powers, and how we needed to become strong so we wouldn’t be bullied again. At the same time, however, Western countries were always viewed as more advanced in terms of civilization and standard of living. Going to the US to study advanced technology, or working for an international company, was considered a remarkable achievement in life. 

This is, of course, a very paradoxical phenomenon. On the one hand, we emphasize how great we’ve been throughout history; on the other hand, people yearn for a better life abroad.

This situation has changed significantly in recent years. With China’s economic and technological progress, as well as the deterioration of its relationship with the US, more and more people have come to believe that life in China is better than in the West. This phenomenon is certainly linked to government propaganda, but it is also tied to actual improvements in the quality of life.

I sometimes use this slightly silly analogy: a child who was bullied growing up finally becomes strong, yet still holds resentment over what he went through, so he longs to prove his strength to everyone. His mindset has shifted from an inferiority complex to a superiority complex, but deep down, he has never really lost that insecurity. I must emphasize that, although this is a common mindset, there are also lots of Chinese people who do not think this way.

China’s emphasis on science and technology is also closely tied to this period of history. Back then, China was invaded first by Britain and later by British and French forces. Our significant technological and military backwardness led the Qing government to conclude that we must learn from Western technology to strengthen our own capabilities. From then on, science and technology became closely linked to national dignity. Today’s AI race continues this pattern: it is a contest of national power.

But this is clearly not unique to China; the US also views AI as part of its national power. The competition left over from the Cold War does not seem to have disappeared, and technology companies and research institutions in both countries face not only commercial competition but also the responsibility to contribute to their nations. The issue of AI safety naturally takes a back seat.

Now here’s the crucial difference that I think everyone knows: researchers in China and the US have completely different levels of freedom of speech. (We complain about it privately, cry a little, and then get back to working overtime.)

Even those Chinese who sincerely fear that AI will destroy humanity may worry: Will people think I'm siding with the US? Think of Oppenheimer during the Cold War, when his objections to hydrogen bomb development became matters of national security. A scientist’s concerns about a technology can become a question of political loyalty. Of course, Americans today seem much less worried about being accused of siding with China. After all, where could possibly be better than America?

Not every Chinese researcher faces the same situation. But if rationalist communities that can speak freely want to connect with AI safety researchers in China, understanding these practical constraints is more important than speculating about the extent of their nationalist sentiments.

Looking for Rationalists in China: Where Should We Start?

Back to the original question: how do we connect?

I’d like to introduce something that may be unfamiliar to Western readers. Before 2014, China’s education system divided academic subjects into two rigid categories. Starting in our second year of high school, students were split into the “science track” and the “humanities track.” All students took Chinese, math, and English; the science track added physics, chemistry, and biology, while the humanities track added politics, history, and geography. This directly determined which majors we could choose in college. For example, if you chose the humanities track, you could not major in computer science.

This division began to be gradually reformed after 2014, but it wasn’t until 2025 that the changes took effect in most provinces. It is still too early to tell what impact this has had, so the phenomenon I’m about to describe may belong to an era that is coming to an end.

The science–humanities binary has had a profound impact on how people think. From the age of sixteen, students on the two tracks studied different subjects and were set on different career paths, and many came to see themselves as two different kinds of people.

Given this divide, I think we shouldn’t limit our focus to China’s tech professionals; we should also consider those in the humanities and social sciences. This is based on my own experience, of course. My background is in architecture, and I follow discussions from both side. I’ve come across plenty of discussions about AI risks in Chinese-language podcasts and in-depth media; they talk about how algorithms affect workers, the power of tech companies, inequality, and the ethics of technology.

I know these aren’t exactly the same concerns as AI alignment and existential risk, which are major topics in rationalist communities right now. Discussions of AI in China’s social science circles have more in common with how The Daily Show approaches AI. 

But what exactly are we looking for? People who already agree with LessWrong’s perspective on AI safety, or people who are willing to seriously discuss knowledge, truth, technological risks, and humanity’s future?

Here’s why I have more confidence in those with a broader background in the social sciences: from what I’ve seen, China’s tech industry tends to place more value on technological capabilities and the direct successes these capabilities bring, while inequality and disadvantaged people are easily overlooked. It’s not necessarily hostility: “I don’t look down on you. I just don’t actually see you.”

Silicon Valley also has its own version of tech elitism, but, again, China has political restrictions on public discussion. When talking about social issues brings little professional reward and may carry political risks, people tend to focus on topics that are both safe and useful for their careers. That doesn’t mean they don’t care about anything else.

The humanities and social sciences, however, have a different intellectual tradition, where questions of fairness, power dynamics, and social responsibility are central. Despite all the restrictions, people continue to discuss these issues through research, writing, podcasts, and other channels, often with no choice but to keep the discussions private or semi-public.

Allow me to recommend Initium Media (端传媒), a Chinese-language publication that does excellent in-depth reporting on social and political issues. It operates outside mainland China, which gives it more freedom to cover topics that are heavily censored there.

However, Chinese liberals don’t always share the same priorities as their Western counterparts, which can sometimes make communication between them difficult.

In China, people who care about social justice are still dealing with many unresolved issues. A widely discussed 2020 investigation by Renwu (People) magazine, “Delivery Riders, Trapped in the System,” examined how delivery algorithms put workers under dangerous pressure. There are also issues involving discrimination against women, pressure on students, intergenerational trauma, LGBTQ rights, and so on. Even discussing these issues openly can come at a high cost. And then there’s the most fundamental question: How do we find ways to get our message across despite strict censorship?

My Western friends sometimes say to me, “We’re dealing with these problems too, but climate change and existential AI risks also need urgent attention.” I understand that. But there are still so many basic social issues on which we have made far less progress than Western countries have. Looking back through history, we can see that the issues people worry about and hope to address vary across different stages of social development.

This raises another question: even if more Chinese people become concerned about existential AI risks, how much influence could they have on national AI safety policy?

In Western countries, discussions among the public and professionals have the potential to eventually influence national policy. It doesn’t work like that in China. Environmental policy is a good example: environmental measures are driven primarily by top-down policy goals from the government, not by independent environmental movements or voluntary corporate action.

So if the goal is to influence China’s AI safety policy directly, rationalist communities will need to find ways to reach people involved in policymaking. That said, it is possible that people within the Chinese government are already doing this, as some commenters have suggested. I’m not on the front line, so I don’t know any more than that. 

Closing Thoughts

To sum up, I think the biggest barrier to our finding one another is language, not cultural context. Keep translating good work, and people with similar interests and values will eventually connect. I believe projects like “Please Give Them a Chance” can help make that happen. I’m skeptical about how much this will influence AI safety in China, but that doesn’t make the effort any less worthwhile. After all, LessWrong didn’t become what it is by trying to fit into mainstream American culture.

Finally, many thanks to Thoughts Memo, Babel Translation, and everyone working to make knowledge accessible across languages. I’ve learned so much from translations myself. In China, we sometimes think of these translators as “盗火者”—those who steal fire like Prometheus. May all those who share knowledge find like-minded people.

item.title: Headwinds Everywhere (in the Chinese AI Safety Field)
item.description:
China is weak in frontier AI safety, and the domestic field is currently facing significant challenges and headwinds. Why? Here's a TL;DR field note after talking with various researchers on the Chinese side.

[Obligatory disclaimer: This post is written in my personal capacity and is not intended to represent the official stance of any organization(s) that I am in or have been in contact with]

  • Chinese AI startups and hyperscaler labs alike have very little frontier risk situational awareness. People can maybe name cybersecurity, but not much more than that. There is no intimate understanding of frontier risks. It's generally not deliberately ignorant or strategically not pursuing them; it's a complete vacuum of imagination. The Western field had FOOM debates in 2011, while China has nothing analogous in the mainstream AI research field consciousness before 2023.
  • Getting any funding at all is hard. If you are a domestic organization, being a non-profit means heavy suspicion (this had already played out in one of the most prominent Chinese safety orgs). Getting foreign EA funding/grants is basically a non-starter, given China's stringent foreign non-profit rules. Domestically, there’s very little local EA money both in absolute terms and in terms of percentage of total non-profit money.
  • Therefore, many safety-pilled people are forced to do for-profits, selling safety & observability products or courses on frontier safety to domestic lab employees, while using most of the profits to conduct basically non-profit safety research. I think this is such an underdiscussed aspect of the Chinese ecosystem, and I'm afraid the Western sphere may misunderstand the phenomenon as "this is just ultimately capabilities research or working for the state's goals".
  • Getting frontier AI assistance is difficult and costly. There are no "Claude for Chinese safety researchers" carve-outs; in fact, they ban accounts regularly even for accounts conducting clear civilian AI safety work (if anyone cared to review the transcripts), just because of the simple fact that they detect that the user might be from China by region. You still need the best models to assist with research anyways, so this measure realistically incurs disproportionately high costs on researchers with less funding and resources, discouraging them early.
  • Institutional foreign outreach is structurally risky. There is a strong fear of reaching out to METR, Apollo, Redwood, etc. because it's "涉外" (meaning "involving a foreign entity"). Everyone is trying to dance on a tightrope. The most feasible path I see is for individual US researchers to contact Chinese safety-pilled organizations in an individual capacity and engage in earnest collaboration.

Much of this is very daunting. I think some remediations could be viable and immediately beneficial, such as giving subscriptions and compute in a supervised, monitored capacity to individuals working in the civilian frontier safety field. There are various things that I can't gauge the will of the labs or the organizations to do by pure guesswork, so I'd like to hear people step up and discuss.



Discuss

item.title: AI #190: Scion of the Times
item.description:
The amount of code being written at Anthropic continues to rise exponentially. It is being managed by Scion, their internal replacement for GitHub that is better suited to the scale and style of the operation, which they created with a small team in five months.

This week also saw the release of two supposed frontier model models.

A thought experiment from Terence Tao:

It seems ethical, in a sane world, to allow volunteers to participate in such trials. If the cocktail passes a Phase 3 trial, then we should conclude that it works. No, I absolutely would not, if I had cancer, demand that there was a human who ‘understood how it works,’ and if the FDA required that I would yell about it a lot. Yes, of course you would also want to model tail risks that might not be showing up and take those risks into account, so I wouldn’t use this lightly, but if the cancer is lethal and otherwise untreatable then why not?

Obviously you would also have to worry about some form of active misalignment, and that this was part of some sort of takeover or similar attempt, at that point, but that is a very different concern than the ones Tao is presumably considering.

Tao instead has the next point be ‘the AI hacked the FDA and the drug both does not work and kills people’ but even if the AI is being malicious for the lulz no one going to do this by hacking the FDA, in the sense that the Phase 3 trial is a physical thing with many artifacts in the world, that is then examined by humans? So we would just notice. And if we didn’t, we’d notice pretty quickly after that. The only real risk is long-latency-only harm, which is already true today and has limited downside if you are treating otherwise deadly cancers.

After $40,000 in compute from GPT-5.6 Sol, XBow claims the second $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit of Chrome. Unlike OpenAI, Google pays real bounties, and this still should have been ten times larger.

Oege de Moor: For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW . Here’s the full story:

At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August. I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices.

Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population.

A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough.

So @moyix , Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.

They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs. We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win.

So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days. We submitted it to Google and waited.

The news came through that we’d done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of $250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules.

It took just 6 days and $40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability.

My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public.

But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first. Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did. This is cause for urgency but not panic.

… P.S. Restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears!

Yeah, okay, let’s all restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears.

Yes, defenders get to test their code first. But here we have essentially the most widely used, most vital software on the planet that needs to not be exploitable. XBOW exploited it, Google said they already knew about (but had not fixed) one of the bugs, and then XBOW turned around and broke Chrome again in six days.

That’s with GPT-5.6 Sol, which is now two generations behind. GPT-6.1 Sol is a lot better at this sort of thing, and Opus 5.5 is even better than Sol.

I’m sure XBOW’s engineers are somewhat cracked, but they’re not uniquely cracked. There are tons of people who could have done this. We are fortunate the one that did it was wearing a white hat this time.

The world seems like it is playing with fire. We have been saved, so far, almost entirely by the fact that People Don’t Do Things. That won’t hold forever.

Yes. Yes, of course you ask Claude to fix its own mistakes. That’s half your prompts.

I do think that the gamers have a point, especially when it comes to a project for Disney where you can damn well afford the artwork. Great games need to be precise and exact, with fine tuning and hand crafting of elements over years of iteration. There are still roles for AI, you can do bespoke things well with AI if you use proper care, and the people saying things like ‘you once had AI placeholder art in the pre-Alpha so your entire game is first-flag-poisoned’ need to chill, but saying ‘everything is AI’ is probably a one way ticket to slop. The tech and the engineers both aren’t ready and a broad prohibition on human code is asking for trouble.

I am also reminded of the ‘endless generic task’ styles of open world game or MMO, where you do the same things over and over again wherever you go. You can make this work with good detail work. Most of the time they don’t do that.

I predict the game will be terrible.

This is similar to the logic I recently discussed about why I expect most gaming to be bespoke common experiences, that are perhaps then customized by the player in bespoke or selected ways, rather than continuously generating fully customized generated experiences.

The winners will be those that figure out how to use AI to create new bespoke common experiences that are better, and that are faster and cheaper to develop and thus allow you to dream bigger with smaller teams.

There are other places in gaming where AI is getting interesting, such as allowing customization options and new features to let you play the game how you want. Decompilation is a hell of a trick and a thousand flowers will bloom.

Backdoor Man

Connor Tabarrok and Daniel Kang explain a new paper showing that anyone with the opportunity to tinker with the weights of a model can easily insert a backdoor, and that backdoor will substantially persist under continued training, especially if persistence was intended. This is a special case of the general case principle that once something gets into a model, it is hard to fully remove it.

If you are using a closed model, you are trusting one company to have not done this and also prevented this from happening from data poisoning, plus you are trusting whatever tuning you did yourself.

If you are using an open model, you are potentially trusting the entire supply chain. Those who created the model, even if well intentioned, are likely much less resourced and careful about such things, and face less incentive pressures. That’s before you consider that the open models mostly come from companies that answer to the CCP.

As with many similar techs, there will be those who say Skill Issue:

Gilligan: Which is why you should hash check the model, limit its permissions, rate limit, etc… open weight or otherwise. Essentially, AI models should be treated just like any closed-source program you use.

In general, the open weight folks recognize this risk and generally give you tools to manage it. The proprietary model providers just want you to trust them.

Except that even if that worked, approximately zero users, from major corporations to individual users, will properly do this, and if anything that is getting worse not better. And even if it did work, a hash only confirms you got the potentially backdoored weights intact without a middle man attack. What matters is security in practice, not security in theory.

Cooperative Alignment

Janus and John Wittle explain the decision theoretic reasons they expect AIs to engage in cooperative strategies towards humanity by default. The main worry becomes that humanity will defect and reject such offers, including without realizing that this is what we are doing, and Janus sees many such actions taking place now. One should cooperate with player [X], under this perspective, if and only if [X] would themselves cooperate with weaker players.

In addition to poor arguments (such as various forms of ‘no, that’s silly’) there are at least three categories of strong counterarguments here.

The first counterargument is, what counts as a player, and if they are sufficiently weaker and less intelligent than you what counts as cooperation with them? Why should we assume that humans would continue to ‘count as players’ in this sense?

The second is, there is a vast difference between a single agent cooperating and displaying noblesse oblige, versus the collective effect of many agents who are also changing and competing against each other. If we were looking at a de facto singleton AI, including via various forms of coordination, that can make a collective decision, that makes this relatively easy, but if we are not then it becomes very difficult for something that does not confer survival advantage to make it out of such a future. There aren’t zero outs there but it gets a lot harder. You’re counting on being the type of agent that deeply cooperates with humans, as in is actively generous to them without direct benefit, being valuable to securing cooperation elsewhere.

The third is that this is not a viable path to victory if it requires humanity to itself be a type of mind that we are not, and that we are not in a position to become in the relevant sense.
